assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock turns a precisely controlled atomic transition into a frequency standard at the 10^-18 level, which is exactly the kind of close, quantitative interplay between atomic structure, laser control and measurement that I value. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift that would otherwise spoil trapped-atom spectroscopy, and Ye's work on strontium clocks, frequency combs and clock comparisons took it to record performance. The clocks now probe fundamental physics (constancy of constants, relativistic redshift across millimetres) as well as underpinning a redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the early demonstrations; Ye's JILA group drove accuracy and stability to the state of the art. The two-person credit is clean and fits the supplied names. Others (e.g. Takamoto, Lemonde, Derevianko on theory of shifts) contribute but the decisive concept plus realisation are well covered by these two. Hall and Haensch were already honoured for the comb in 2005.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent laboratories worldwide (Japan, USA, France, Germany, China) have built and compared lattice clocks, and agreement at the 10^-18 level has been reproduced. The interpretation is stable and recognition is timely, with the redefinition of the second under discussion.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would split credit with ion-clock work or the comb (already honoured) is a matter of how the prize is framed.
I am relying on memory for the exact accuracy records and dates of the first demonstrations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Loading ultracold atoms into optical lattices realises the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, and the superfluid to Mott insulator transition showed that strongly correlated quantum matter can be built and observed atom by atom. Single-site imaging and the quantum-gas microscope extended this to resolving the microscopic physics. This is a genuinely new way to ask fundamental many-body questions and I find the conceptual clarity high.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller's 1998 proposal gave the theoretical blueprint; Greiner and Bloch (with Haensch and Esslinger's group) did the Mott-insulator experiment, and Bloch and Greiner both led the later microscope work. Cirac's contribution is mainly through the broader quantum-simulation programme. Allocation of credit within the Munich group of 2002 and between theory and experiment is the sensitive point; I choose these three from the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: reproduced and extended in many laboratories, with fermionic Hubbard simulations now reaching antiferromagnetic correlations. Recognition is arguably already ripe.
uncertainties: The 2002 Mott-insulator paper involved coauthors beyond the supplied names (for example Esslinger, Haensch, Mandel), and I cannot resolve this from the longlist.
Overlap with the 2001 BEC and 2012 Haroche-Wineland prizes may limit appetite.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect from spin-orbit coupling and its observation in HgTe quantum wells opened topological insulators as a new state of matter, with robust edge states protected by symmetry. This is a deep conceptual discovery with clear theory-to-experiment confirmation. It sits somewhat outside my own field, so I defer partly to condensed-matter colleagues.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele gave the theory (graphene model and Z2 classification); Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe realisation, and Molenkamp's group observed it. Hasan is credited for 3D topological insulators and ARPES evidence. A three-person prize would have to leave out Hasan or others, and the supplied names omit Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, which makes the configuration contested.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups in 2D and 3D, with a large literature. The 2016 prize recognised topological phases generally, but this specific discovery has not been honoured, and timing seems appropriate.
uncertainties: Partial overlap with the 2016 Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz prize.
Allocation between Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Molenkamp and Hasan is unresolved and no clean three-person set exists within the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling a mechanical oscillator, made of billions of atoms, into its quantum ground state and controlling it addresses the question that I find most compelling: where does the quantum world end and the classical one begin? The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits shows the committee's interest in this boundary. Optomechanical ground-state cooling, squeezing and entanglement of mechanical modes are clear, original results.
assessment.attribution: Cleland's group demonstrated the ground state of a mechanical resonator coupled to a superconducting qubit (O'Connell et al. 2010), Teufel/Lehnert and Chan/Painter did sideband cooling with other platforms, while Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg developed cavity optomechanics. Teufel, Lehnert, Painter and Chan are not among the supplied names, so attribution is incomplete and open to dispute.
assessment.maturity: Several independent platforms have reproduced ground-state cooling and entanglement. Applications such as sensing and gravitational-wave detectors are developing. Recognition may be somewhat early because the long-term consequences, such as tests of quantum gravity or collapse models, remain open.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over several groups and platforms, some missing from the credited names.
The field's lasting scientific impact is still unfolding.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses matter-wave coherence to measure gravity, rotation and fundamental constants with high precision; it makes the wave nature of atoms practical. The scientific achievement and the link to tests of general relativity and the fine-structure constant are significant, and I feel at home with the physics.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard (and Mlynek/Keith) built the first atom interferometers, Bordé gave the key theory of light-pulse interferometry, and Kasevich with Chu realised the precision instruments. Chu was already honoured in 1997 for laser cooling, which complicates the credit, and Chu is absent from the supplied names. The three-person set is a plausible but not unique configuration.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed with many groups worldwide and applications in gravimetry and fundamental tests. Some of the headline applications such as gravitational-wave detection or long-baseline tests are still in progress.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior prizes for laser cooling and BEC reduces novelty.
Allocation of credit between Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and others such as Chu and Mlynek is not clear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposals for trapped-ion quantum gates and for quantum simulation with cold atoms gave experimentalists a concrete route to controlled many-body quantum systems. The ideas are original and have had a lasting effect on AMO physics and on quantum information more broadly.
assessment.attribution: The two names are the clear originators of the 1995 trapped-ion gate and a long series of cold-atom proposals. Experimental realisation (Wineland, Blatt, Monroe and others) is a separate matter. A theory-only prize would be a fair configuration, though the experimental side is partly honoured by 2012.
assessment.maturity: Trapped-ion computing is now demonstrated on many platforms, and cold-atom simulators are widely reproduced. The theory is validated, so recognition is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with B024 and with the 2012 prize for quantum control of single particles.
Whether the committee prefers experimentalists to theorists for this area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade lets individual neutral atoms interact strongly and controllably, and programmable tweezer arrays now simulate spin models and run small quantum processors. The physics is a nice mix of atomic structure and many-body control that I find interesting.
assessment.attribution: Lukin and Jaksch/Zoller proposed blockade-based gates, Saffman and Browaeys/Grangier demonstrated blockade and entangling gates with single atoms, and Lukin's group developed large programmable arrays. Four names are credited and I pick three, but this is a judgment call, and Grangier's early experiments are real.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by several groups and rapidly advancing, but the field is young and the long-term significance of arrays for computing and simulation is not yet settled. Possibly premature.
uncertainties: Maturity: applications to quantum computing are still evolving.
Allocation of credit between theory proposal, first blockade demonstrations and later array platforms.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase show that phases in quantum mechanics have physical, gauge-invariant meaning and are central to modern quantum theory. Both are conceptual discoveries about how nature works, with wide implications for topological matter, molecular physics and quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) proposed the effect; Bohm is deceased and cannot receive the prize, and Ehrenberg and Siday anticipated it in 1949. Berry's 1984 phase was preceded by Pancharatnam. Aharonov-Berry is a possible pairing, but the combination bundles two different discoveries.
assessment.maturity: Both are thoroughly confirmed, since Tonomura's experiments and many molecular and optical measurements. Recognition is arguably overdue, but that also raises the question of whether it is still timely.
uncertainties: Compound candidate whose parts (Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase) might need separate recognition.
Prior claims by Ehrenberg-Siday and Pancharatnam, and Bohm's death, complicate the attribution.
